categories.intro: Hydraulic adapters are fittings that join one connection type to another — a different thread form, size, seat or direction — so that a hose, tube or component can meet a port it was not made for. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics carbon-steel and stainless adapters from Dubai in BSP, metric, JIS, NPT, JIC 37°, ORFS, SAE O-ring boss, DIN 2353 bite-type and SAE flange forms: straight connectors, 45° and 90° elbows, adjustable stud ends, run and branch tees, crosses, bulkheads, swivels, plugs and caps.

faq.q: How do I tell BSP, JIC, ORFS and metric apart?
faq.a: By the seat and the thread together. JIC seals on a 37° flare with a UN/UNF thread; ORFS seals on an O-ring in a flat face, also on a UN thread; BSP hydraulic ends usually seal on a 60° cone with a Whitworth-form thread; metric 24° cone ends seal on the cone. Measure the thread diameter and pitch, look at the seat, and send a photo if in doubt.

faq.q: Is an adapter rated as high as the hose?
faq.a: Not automatically. Each adapter has its own working pressure by size and form, and a tapered thread end in particular can be rated well below the hose. A circuit is limited by its lowest-rated component.

faq.q: Do you stock adapters for Japanese machines?
faq.a: Yes — JIS gas and JIS metric 60° cone adapters for Japanese-built machines, and metric adapters made to Komatsu’s specification.

faq.q: How do I read a title like “Adjustable Branch Tee m ORFS X m BSP X m ORFS”?
faq.a: Each end is named in turn, with m for a male end and f for a female end. In a tee, the ends are usually listed run, branch, run, so that title is an adjustable tee with ORFS male ends on the run and a BSP male on the branch. “Adjustable” means the stud end carries a locknut and O-ring, so the body can be turned to any direction before it is locked. Check the drawing on the listing to confirm which end is which before ordering, especially on run tees, where the odd end sits on the run rather than the branch.

faq.q: How do I fit an adjustable stud-end elbow or tee?
faq.a: Wind the locknut back fully, screw the stud in by hand until the backup washer meets the port face, back it out by no more than one turn to point it where you need, then hold the body and tighten the locknut. Lubricate the O-ring with system fluid first, and check it has not been cut on the thread. Turning the body back the other way after the washer is seated, or tightening the locknut without holding the body, are the usual causes of a leak at the port.

faq.q: Can I reuse an adapter when a line is remade?
faq.a: Often, if its sealing surfaces are undamaged, but the seals are renewed. O-rings, bonded seals and ED seals are replaced every time the joint is opened. Flare and cone seats can be remade if they show no nicks, radial scratches or distortion. Taper threads (NPT, BSPT) seal by deforming, so each remake goes a little deeper and a heavily reused taper end should be replaced. A bite-type ring stays on its own tube end. Discard any adapter with a cracked body, a stripped or galled thread or a coined seat.

categories.intro: Hydraulic hose fittings are the end connections crimped or swaged onto a hydraulic hose so that it can be joined to a port, adapter or tube. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics hose ends from Dubai for braided (1SN, 2SN) and spiral (4SP, R12) hose: BSP 60° cone and flat seat, DIN light and heavy 24° cone, JIC 37°, ORFS, NPT, SAE 45° flare, SAE Code 61 and Code 62 flange heads, Komatsu, Toyota and JIS forms, banjos, and pressure-washer ends, straight and in 45° and 90° elbows.

faq.q: What is the difference between braided-hose and spiral-hose fittings?
faq.a: The tail. Spiral hose has four or six wire layers and a thicker wall, so its fittings use a heavier body and usually a skived ferrule that grips the wire directly. The port end can be identical; the hose end is not interchangeable.

faq.q: Skive or no-skive?
faq.a: Whichever the hose and fitting series are designed for. Skive ferrules need the outer cover — and sometimes the inner tube — removed so the ferrule grips the wire; no-skive ferrules crimp over the cover. Use the ferrule specified for the construction; the two are designed together.

faq.q: How do I measure a hose fitting thread?
faq.a: Measure across the crests of a male thread (or inside a female), measure the pitch — threads per inch, or millimetres between crests — and look at the seat: a 37° flare, a 24° or 60° cone, or a flat face with an O-ring. Diameter, pitch and seat together identify the family. Send them with a photo and we will confirm.

faq.q: Should I choose a swivel or a rigid hose fitting?
faq.a: Use a swivel female wherever you can: its nut turns independently, so the joint is made up without twisting the hose. A rigid male end can only be screwed in by turning the whole assembly, so it is normally fitted first, or mated to a swivel female at the other side. A hose installed with twist in it loses a large part of its life, because the wire reinforcement is loaded unevenly. If both ends must be rigid, add a swivel adapter at one port.

faq.q: How do I measure the length of a hose assembly for a replacement?
faq.a: Measure overall length from the end of one fitting to the end of the other: to the sealing face on straight ends, and to the centreline of the sealing face on elbows. Do not measure the hose alone, because the fittings add a different length for each style. Lay the old assembly straight to measure it, and tell us the length, the two fittings, the hose bore and construction, and the elbow orientation if there are two elbows.

faq.q: What is elbow orientation on a hose assembly with two elbows?
faq.a: It is the angle between the two elbows, measured looking along the hose from one end, and it must be specified or the assembly will arrive twisted to fit. Hold the assembly with the far elbow pointing straight away from you and read the angle, clockwise, to the near elbow: 0° means both point the same way. Fitting a wrongly oriented assembly by twisting the hose shortens its life. Send the angle, or a photo of the old assembly laid flat, with your enquiry.

categories.intro: BSP hydraulic adapters are fittings with British Standard Pipe threads — parallel (BSPP) or taper (BSPT) — used to connect hoses, tubes and components on European- and Asian-built machinery. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics BSP adapters from Dubai with 60° cone, bonded-seal, O-ring and taper ends: straight connectors, unions, 45° and 90° elbows, tees, crosses, bulkheads, plugs, caps and butt-weld ends, plus BSP adapters to metric, JIC, NPT and JIS gas.

faq.q: Can I use a BSPT fitting in a BSPP port?
faq.a: It will engage but it will not seal reliably: a parallel port is sealed by a cone, a bonded seal or an O-ring, not by thread interference. Use a parallel male with the correct seal for the port.

faq.q: What is a bonded seal?
faq.a: A steel washer with a moulded rubber lip — often called a Dowty washer — that seals a parallel thread against a flat face.

faq.q: What is an ED seal?
faq.a: An elastomer seal carried in the stud end of the adapter, which seals against the port face and removes the need for a separate washer.

faq.q: Why is a 1/2″ BSP thread about 21 mm across?
faq.a: Because the nominal size refers to an old pipe bore, not to the thread. A 1/2″ BSP male measures about 20.96 mm over the crests with 14 threads per inch. Other common sizes: 1/8″ is 9.73 mm at 28 TPI, 1/4″ 13.16 mm at 19 TPI, 3/8″ 16.66 mm at 19 TPI, 3/4″ 26.44 mm at 14 TPI and 1″ 33.25 mm at 11 TPI. BSPP and BSPT share these diameters and pitches, so measure the crests with calipers, count the pitch, then check for taper.

faq.q: What does “60° Seat or Bonded Seal” mean on a BSP male?
faq.a: It is a dual-purpose male end: its nose has a 60° cone that seals in a BSP female swivel, and its shoulder has a flat face that seals against a port with a bonded seal. One part therefore covers both a hose-end connection and a flat-faced BSPP port. Use the bonded seal only in the port; in a 60° cone female the seal is metal to metal and no washer is needed.

faq.q: Should a BSPT thread get tape or sealant?
faq.a: Yes — a taper thread seals on its flanks and needs a thread sealant or PTFE tape; a parallel BSPP thread never does. Keep the first one or two threads clear so nothing is carried into the system, and wrap tape in the direction of the thread. Liquid or paste sealants rated for hydraulic oil are cleaner than tape. Sealant on a BSPP thread can stop a bonded seal or O-ring seating and is a common cause of leaks.

categories.intro: Metric hydraulic adapters are fittings with metric fine threads that connect ports, tubes and hose ends sealed by an O-ring, a bonded seal, a flat face or a cone. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics metric adapters from Dubai in sizes M10×1 to M42×2: ISO 6149 O-ring studs, flat-seal and bonded-seal studs, 74° cone and JIS 60° cone ends, Komatsu-specification connectors, butt-weld ends, plugs and caps, as straight connectors, elbows, tees, crosses, bulkheads and adjustable stud ends.

faq.q: How do I tell an ISO 6149 port from a DIN 3852 port?
faq.a: An ISO 6149 port has a raised identification ring on its spot-face and seals on an O-ring in a truncated housing. A DIN 3852 port is a plain spot-face sealed by a bonded or elastomer seal on the stud end.

faq.q: Are JIS metric and DIN metric ends interchangeable?
faq.a: No. JIS metric ends seal on a 60° cone and DIN metric ends on a 24° cone; the threads can look alike, but the seats are different.

faq.q: Do you stock Komatsu adapters?
faq.a: Yes — metric adapters made to Komatsu’s specification sit on this shelf alongside the standard ranges.

faq.q: Which thread sizes does an ISO 6149 metric port use?
faq.a: ISO 6149-1 ports run from M8×1 up to M60×2. The common hydraulic sizes are M10×1, M12×1.5, M14×1.5, M16×1.5, M18×1.5, M20×1.5, M22×1.5, M27×2, M33×2 and M42×2. Measure the outside diameter of the male thread and the distance between crests to read it, then look for the raised identification ring on the port spot-face to confirm it is ISO 6149 rather than a plain DIN face port of the same thread.

faq.q: What is a butt-weld tube end on a metric adapter for?
faq.a: It is a plain end machined to be butt-welded to steel tube, so a welded pipework system can be joined to a metric port or fitting. Remove every O-ring and seal before welding and fit them after the part has cooled, because the heat destroys elastomers. Match the adapter material and wall to the tube, and clean scale out of the bore before the line goes into service.

faq.q: Which way round do I fit an adjustable metric elbow?
faq.a: Fit the stud end into the port first, then connect the tube or hose to the other end. Back the locknut off fully, screw the elbow in by hand until the washer touches the port face, turn it back no more than one turn to aim it, then hold the body and tighten the locknut. Making up the line end first and then winding the stud in twists the line and can cut the O-ring.

categories.intro: Stainless steel hydraulic fittings are hose ends, adapters and flanges machined from SS316L for lines where zinc-plated carbon steel corrodes: offshore, washdown, chemical and coastal plant. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics SS316L fittings from Dubai in BSP 60° cone and flat seat, metric 24° cone, JIC 37°, ORFS, NPT and NPSM forms, double-hex swivels, SAE Code 61 and Code 62 flanges with seals, banjos, standpipes and hydrowashing couplings.

faq.q: Is 316L stainless rated as high as carbon steel?
faq.a: Not always. A stainless fitting can carry a lower working pressure than a carbon-steel part of the same size and form, so check the rating on the listing against the line rather than assuming the carbon-steel figure.

faq.q: Can stainless fittings be used with carbon-steel adapters?
faq.a: They will connect, but in a wet or salty environment the joint becomes a galvanic cell and the less noble part corrodes faster. Match materials where the exposure is severe.

faq.q: Do you supply material certificates?
faq.a: Ask for EN 10204 material certificates at quotation if your order needs them, and we will confirm what is available for each item.

faq.q: Why 316L rather than 304 stainless?
faq.a: 316L contains molybdenum, which gives it much better resistance to pitting in chlorides — seawater, salt air and many cleaning chemicals — than 304. The L means low carbon, which limits carbide formation when the part is welded, so welded standpipes and weld fittings keep their corrosion resistance at the joint. For Gulf coastal and offshore service, 316L is the usual minimum grade.

faq.q: Will 316L fittings rust on a coastal site?
faq.a: They can show surface staining in hot, salty air, but they do not corrode through the way plated carbon steel does. Brown tea-staining on 316L in the Gulf is common where salt deposits sit on the surface and are never washed off, and crevices under clamps and tags are where it starts. Rinsing with fresh water during routine maintenance largely prevents it; heavy pitting points to a harsher environment and a higher grade.

faq.q: How can I tell a stainless fitting from plated steel?
faq.a: A magnet is the quickest check: plated carbon steel is strongly magnetic, while 316L is essentially non-magnetic. Cold-worked or machined areas of stainless can pull slightly, so a weak attraction is not proof of steel. Plated steel also shows yellow or silver zinc plating that wears through to grey at edges and threads. For a documented check, ask for the material certificate when you order.

categories.intro: DIN 2353 bite-type adapters are 24° cone tube fittings in which a hardened cutting ring bites into the outside of metric steel tube as the nut is tightened, sealing on the cone. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics bite-type fittings from Dubai to DIN 2353 / ISO 8434-1 in light and heavy series: male stud connectors and elbows with BSPP, BSPT, NPT and metric ends, unions, elbows, tees, crosses, bulkheads, adjustable stud ends, weld connectors, banjos, nuts, cutting rings and blanking plugs.

faq.q: Can I mix L and S series parts?
faq.a: No. For the same tube size the two series use different nut threads, and their pressure ratings differ. Identify the series from the existing parts before ordering.

faq.q: Do I need a new cutting ring when I remake a joint?
faq.a: A ring that has already bitten can be remade on the same tube end, but it should never be moved to a different tube. When the tube is cut back, fit a new ring.

faq.q: Do you supply blanking plugs?
faq.a: Yes — blanking plugs for cones, plugs for ports with ED seals, and plugs with nuts.

faq.q: Which nut thread goes with which tube size?
faq.a: Each tube OD and series has its own nut thread. Light series: 6L M12×1.5, 8L M14×1.5, 10L M16×1.5, 12L M18×1.5, 15L M22×1.5, 18L M26×1.5, 22L M30×2, 28L M36×2, 35L M45×2, 42L M52×2. Heavy series: 6S M14×1.5, 8S M16×1.5, 10S M18×1.5, 12S M20×1.5, 14S M22×1.5, 16S M24×1.5, 20S M30×2, 25S M36×2, 30S M42×2, 38S M52×2. Note that 12L and 10S share M18×1.5, so a thread that fits does not prove the tube size: check the tube OD too.

faq.q: What does a code like GE 12 L R1/2 mean?
faq.a: It is the DIN-style designation many makers use: the body type, the tube OD in millimetres, the series, then the port thread. GE is a male stud connector, so GE 12 L R1/2 is a straight stud connector for 12 mm tube, light series, with a 1/2″ BSP thread. Other common prefixes are WE (male stud elbow), GV (straight union), W (union elbow), T (union tee), K (union cross) and SV (bulkhead union). Suffixes for the stud seal and material vary by maker, so send the full code.

faq.q: What tube should be used with bite-type fittings?
faq.a: Seamless precision steel tube to EN 10305-4 (formerly DIN 2391/2445), annealed or normalised so it is softer than the cutting ring, with the OD matching the fitting. Cut the tube square with a saw guide or cutter, deburr inside and out, and check the wall is thick enough for the pressure. Thin-wall or soft tube needs a reinforcing insert so the ring has something to bite against. Make up the ring until it grips, then the further turn the maker specifies, commonly about one and a half.

categories.intro: JIC adapters are 37° flare fittings with UN/UNF threads, sealing metal to metal on the flare, used to join hose, tube and ports on North American and much international machinery. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics JIC adapters from Dubai: JIC to JIC, NPT, BSP, BSPT, metric, metric flat-seal and SAE O-ring boss, as straight connectors, swivels, 45° and 90° elbows, adjustable stud ends, run and branch tees, crosses, bulkheads with locknuts, plugs and caps.

faq.q: What does the dash size mean?
faq.a: The nominal size in sixteenths of an inch: a -08 is 8/16, or 1/2 inch nominal. On a JIC end it identifies the thread — a -08 is 3/4-16 UNF — rather than the bore exactly.

faq.q: Can I tighten a JIC joint harder to stop a leak?
faq.a: No. The seal is the flare, and over-tightening damages it. Make the joint up by flats from finger tight, and if a correctly made joint still weeps, inspect the flare for scratches or distortion.

faq.q: Is JIC the same as SAE 45° flare?
faq.a: No. They share threads on several sizes, but JIC seals on a 37° flare and SAE 45° on a 45° flare. A joint mixing the two may hold briefly, then leak.

faq.q: Why choose a JIC × SAE O-ring boss adapter rather than JIC × NPT for a port?
faq.a: Because an O-ring boss seals on an elastomer O-ring, not on the thread, so it can be remade without losing engagement and, in adjustable form, aimed in any direction. An NPT end seals by thread interference, is rated lower than the O-ring boss in larger sizes, and goes deeper every time it is remade. Note that an O-ring boss end uses the same UN thread as the JIC end of the same dash size: tell them apart by the O-ring at the shoulder.

faq.q: How is a JIC bulkhead adapter fitted through a panel?
faq.a: The long threaded body passes through a hole in the panel and is clamped by the bulkhead locknut, which tightens against the panel rather than sealing anything. Size the hole for the thread with a small clearance and keep the panel within the thickness the body can take. Hold the body while tightening the locknut, then make up the lines on each side by flats as for any JIC joint.

faq.q: How do I blank off a JIC line or port?
faq.a: Use a JIC plug in a female swivel nut and a JIC swivel cap on a male end; both seal on the 37° flare in the same way as a working joint. Make them up by flats from finger tight like any JIC connection, not harder. For a port rather than a hose or tube end, blank it with a plug for that port type, such as an O-ring boss or BSP plug.

faq.q: Are these 316 stainless?
faq.a: Most families are 316L stainless steel, forged; each listing states the grade the manufacturer gives. Where a listing says stainless steel without a grade, ask and we will confirm before you order.

faq.q: Do the listings show dimensions and equivalents?
faq.a: Yes, where the manufacturer publishes them. Every size is listed with its end sizes; most also carry millimetre dimensions and the Parker part number the manufacturer cross-references.

faq.q: Will a stainless JIC adapter mate with a carbon-steel one?
faq.a: Yes, the 37° flare is the same; mixing materials in a wet line can cause galvanic corrosion, so most specifications keep a stainless line stainless.

faq.q: What do I need to connect stainless tube to a JIC adapter?
faq.a: A JIC tube nut and tube sleeve for the tube OD, and a 37° flare on the tube end made with a flaring tool. Slide the nut and sleeve on before flaring, then make the joint up on the male 37° cone. The sleeve supports the tube behind the flare and reduces vibration fatigue. Use annealed stainless tube that will flare without cracking, and check the flare for splits before assembly.

faq.q: What is the difference between a JIC male union and a female swivel union?
faq.a: A male union has a 37° cone at each end and joins two female swivel nuts — two hoses, or two flared tubes. A female swivel union has a swivel nut at each end and joins two male cones. Choose by what is already on the two ends you are joining. Bulkhead unions do the same job through a panel.

faq.q: How do I change dash size on a stainless JIC line?
faq.a: Use a JIC female swivel × JIC male reducer or expander: the swivel end mates the existing male, and the male end takes the new size. A short version is listed where space is tight. Changing size in the line rather than the hose end keeps a standard hose assembly, but every extra joint is a leak path, so where the hose is being replaced anyway, order it with the correct end.

categories.intro: ORFS adapters are O-ring face seal fittings that seal on an O-ring held in a groove in the flat face of the male end, used on hydraulic lines that see vibration and pressure spikes. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics ORFS adapters from Dubai in sizes -04 to -16: ORFS to ORFS, BSP, NPT, metric, metric flat-seal and SAE O-ring boss, as straight and swivel connectors, 45° and 90° elbows, adjustable stud ends, run and branch tees, crosses, bulkheads with locknuts, plugs and caps.

faq.q: Does an ORFS joint need sealant or tape?
faq.a: No — it seals on the face O-ring. Sealant on the thread or the face can stop the O-ring seating, and it contaminates the system.

faq.q: Which O-ring does an ORFS fitting use?
faq.a: A face O-ring sized for the fitting’s dash size, usually nitrile for mineral oil. Use the size specified for the fitting: one too thick or too thin will not seal.

faq.q: Why choose ORFS over JIC?
faq.a: ORFS tolerates vibration better because the seal is an elastomer rather than a metal seat. JIC is simpler and has no O-ring to replace. Most machines use one or the other; match what is fitted.

faq.q: Why won’t an ORFS -08 screw onto a JIC -08?
faq.a: Because ORFS uses a larger thread than JIC at the same dash size. ORFS threads are -04 9/16-18, -06 11/16-16, -08 13/16-16, -10 1-14, -12 1-3/16-12 and -16 1-7/16-12, whereas a JIC -08 is 3/4-16. The dash number gives the tube size, not the thread, so measure the thread and look for the face O-ring before ordering a replacement.

faq.q: Why does an ORFS joint leak when the line is pulled into place?
faq.a: Because the two flat faces must meet square, and a side load lifts one edge of the O-ring off its face. Unlike a cone, a flat face does not centre itself, so the line has to be routed and supported to reach the port without being forced. Seat the O-ring fully in its groove, start the nut by hand, bring the faces together squarely, then tighten to the specified torque.

faq.q: What does “captive seal” mean on an ORFS × metric adapter?
faq.a: It means the stud end’s seal sits in a retaining groove so it cannot fall out or be lost during assembly. The seal faces the port spot-face, so the thread itself carries no sealing duty and no sealant is needed. Replace the seal when the adapter is removed; a nicked or flattened seal is the usual cause of a weep at that end.

categories.intro: Braided hose crimp fittings are one-piece hose ends, with the ferrule attached, that are crimped onto one- or two-wire-braid hydraulic hose. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics fittings from Dubai for EN 853 1SN and 2SN and SAE 100R1AT, 100R2AT, 100R16 and 100R17 hose, with BSP 60° cone, DIN light and heavy 24° cone, JIC 37°, ORFS, SAE 45° flare, NPT, SAE O-ring boss, JIS and Komatsu ends and SAE Code 61 and Code 62 flange heads, straight and in 45° and 90° elbows.

faq.q: Do these fittings need a separate ferrule?
faq.a: No — they are one-piece crimp fittings with the ferrule attached. Crimp them to the diameter specified for the hose and fitting together, on a crimper with the matching dies.

faq.q: Which hose constructions do they suit?
faq.a: EN 853 1SN and 2SN, and SAE 100R1AT, 100R2AT, 100R16 and 100R17. For four- or six-spiral hose use the spiral-hose range: the tails are not interchangeable.

faq.q: How do I cross a Parker part number?
faq.a: Each listing names the Parker series it replaces, and its size table gives our part number for every size. Send the Parker number if you have it and we will confirm the match.

faq.q: Can the port end be a different size from the hose?
faq.a: Yes — the tail must match the hose bore, but many fittings are made with a smaller or larger port end, such as a -08 hose with a -06 JIC end. The size table on each listing gives the hose size and port size separately. A reduced end restricts flow, so check it against the line before choosing it, and confirm the reduced end is rated for the working pressure.

faq.q: How do I check that a braided-hose fitting is crimped correctly?
faq.a: Measure the crimp diameter with calipers across the flats of the ferrule at several points and compare it with the figure the crimp chart gives for that hose and fitting. Check the hose is fully inserted — a mark on the cover at the insertion depth shows if it has moved — and that the ferrule is crimped evenly without a bell or a split. Then pressure-test the assembly before it goes into service.

faq.q: Do R16 and R17 hose take the same fittings as 2SN?
faq.a: Only where the listing names them. R16 and R17 are compact braided hoses with a smaller outside diameter than 2SN of the same bore, so the crimp diameter differs even where the fitting body is shared. Read the hose layline, pick a fitting listed for that construction, and crimp to the chart diameter for that exact hose.

categories.intro: Spiral hose crimp fittings are one-piece hose ends built on a heavier body for four-spiral-wire hydraulic hose, where the pressure and impulse loads exceed what braided hose carries. This shelf carries Indus Hydraulics fittings from Dubai for EN 856 4SP and SAE 100R12 hose, with BSP 60° cone, DIN light and heavy 24° cone, JIC 37°, ORFS, SAE 45° flare, NPT, SAE O-ring boss, JIS and Komatsu ends and SAE Code 61 and Code 62 flange heads, straight and in 45° and 90° elbows.

faq.q: Can I use these on 4SH or R13 hose?
faq.a: They are listed for 4SP and R12. 4SH, R13 and R15 are higher-pressure constructions with their own fittings and ferrules — tell us the hose and we will confirm the correct series.

faq.q: Why are spiral-hose fittings heavier?
faq.a: Spiral hose carries higher pressures and impulse loads, and its thicker wall and wire layers need a longer, stronger grip. The heavier body and its crimp are designed for that construction.

faq.q: Are these one-piece fittings?
faq.a: Yes. Crimp them to the diameter specified for the hose and fitting, with the matching dies.

faq.q: Why do larger spiral hose assemblies use flange heads instead of threaded ends?
faq.a: Because at -16 and above a threaded swivel needs very high torque to seal, is hard to make up in the field and is more likely to loosen under impulse. An SAE Code 61 or Code 62 flange head seals on an O-ring clamped by four bolts, which is easier to assemble on large high-pressure lines and can be released without turning the hose. Code 62 is the higher-pressure pattern; the two are not interchangeable.

faq.q: How close to the fitting can spiral hose bend?
faq.a: Not at the fitting itself: leave a straight length of hose behind the ferrule before the bend starts, and never bend tighter than the hose’s minimum bend radius. A bend that starts at the ferrule concentrates strain on the wire where it leaves the crimp, which is where spiral assemblies usually fail. Where the routing turns sharply at the port, use a 45° or 90° elbow fitting instead of bending the hose.

faq.q: Can a crimped spiral hose fitting be reused?
faq.a: No. The ferrule is permanently deformed onto the hose and its grip cannot be restored once it is cut off, so the fitting is scrapped with the hose. Recrimping a used fitting onto new hose is a known cause of blow-offs. Keep the old assembly for its length and orientation, and order new fittings for the replacement.

faq.q: Are these 316 stainless?
faq.a: Most families are 316L stainless steel, forged; each listing states the grade the manufacturer gives. Where a listing says stainless steel without a grade, ask and we will confirm before you order.

faq.q: Do the listings show dimensions and equivalents?
faq.a: Yes, where the manufacturer publishes them. Every size is listed with its end sizes; most also carry millimetre dimensions and the Parker part number the manufacturer cross-references.

faq.q: What is the extra-light (LL) series for?
faq.a: It is the smallest DIN 2353 series, for small-bore tube in low-pressure, lubrication and instrument lines, and it uses its own nuts, rings and bodies. LL parts do not interchange with L or S parts, even where a thread looks close. Order nut, cutting ring and body together in LL and check the tube OD against the listing.

faq.q: How do I stop a stainless bite-type fitting from galling?
faq.a: Lubricate the nut thread and the cutting ring with a suitable assembly lubricant before make-up, and tighten steadily rather than in jerks. Stainless on stainless is prone to galling, which raises the torque and can seize the nut before the ring has bitten. Pre-setting the ring with a hardened pre-assembly tool gives the most reliable bite on stainless tube.

faq.q: Which stainless tube suits these fittings?
faq.a: Seamless annealed stainless tube, such as 316L, with an OD that matches the fitting and a hardness low enough for the cutting ring to bite. Hard or cold-worked tube resists the ring and can leak or pull out. Cut it square, deburr inside and out, and fit a reinforcing insert in thin-wall tube.

faq.q: What is a soft-seal tube cap?
faq.a: It is a cap that closes the end of a tube, sealing with an elastomer seal so it can be fitted without setting a cutting ring. Use it to blank a tube line temporarily for testing or during maintenance. To blank the fitting body instead, use a tube plug of the same series.

categories.intro: Hydraulic quick couplers are two-part connectors that join and separate a fluid line by hand, sealing each half on disconnection where valved. This shelf carries quick couplers from Dubai for ISO 7241 Series A and B, ISO 16028 flush face, ISO 5675 tractor, HTMA tool, 10,000 psi jack and water-blast, thread-to-connect, ARO 210 and MIL-C-4109 air, SAE J1502 test-point, refrigerant and oil-sampling service, plus a pressure gauge test kit.

faq.q: Will an ISO 7241 Series A coupler connect to Series B?
faq.a: No. Series A and Series B are different interchanges with different dimensions; a coupler connects only to a mating half of the same series and size.

faq.q: When should I use a flush-face coupler?
faq.a: Where dirt and spills matter: construction attachments, mobile machinery and anywhere the coupler is connected in the field. The flat faces wipe clean before connection and trap very little oil when disconnected.

faq.q: Can a coupler be connected under pressure?
faq.a: Only one designed for it. Standard couplers should be connected with both sides depressurised; connect-under-pressure designs, such as the farm coupler on this shelf, are made to connect against residual pressure.

faq.q: Can I mate couplers from two different makers?
faq.a: Yes, if both halves are made to the same interchange standard and size, such as ISO 16028 or ISO 7241 Series A. The standard fixes the mating dimensions, not flow, pressure drop or valve design, so a mixed pair may perform below either maker’s rating. Couplers sold as a maker’s own pattern, with no published interchange, only mate with that maker’s halves.

faq.q: Is a 1/2″ coupler a 1/2″ thread?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The nominal size refers to the coupler body under its interchange standard, and the port thread on the back can be a different size and form — BSP, NPT, SAE O-ring boss or metric. Specify the interchange, the body size and the end thread separately, and check the flow at the body size.

faq.q: When should I choose a thread-to-connect coupler?
faq.a: Where the line sees high pressure, heavy impulse or vibration that can work a push-to-connect sleeve loose, as on hydraulic hammers, breakers and some attachments. The halves are drawn together by a threaded sleeve rather than held by balls, so they stay connected under pressure spikes. They take longer to connect, so use push-to-connect where frequent changes matter more.

faq.q: Are these 316 stainless?
faq.a: Most families are 316L stainless steel, forged; each listing states the grade the manufacturer gives. Where a listing says stainless steel without a grade, ask and we will confirm before you order.

faq.q: Do the listings show dimensions and equivalents?
faq.a: Yes, where the manufacturer publishes them. Every size is listed with its end sizes; most also carry millimetre dimensions and the Parker part number the manufacturer cross-references.

faq.q: What does dual-purpose mean on a stainless JIC × metric adapter?
faq.a: The metric male end can take a DIN 2353 tube nut and cutting ring on its 24° cone, or screw into a metric port with a seal. One part therefore connects a JIC line to either a metric tube or a metric port. Fit a bonded seal or the specified seal when it goes into a port; it is not needed for the tube connection.

faq.q: When should I choose a Viton bonded seal?
faq.a: When the joint runs hot or carries a fluid that attacks nitrile, such as many synthetic and phosphate-ester fluids. A Viton (FKM) ring in a stainless washer suits higher temperatures than standard nitrile. Check the fluid against the seal maker’s compatibility chart; FKM is not suitable for every fluid either.

faq.q: Why use a stainless bonded seal rather than a standard one?
faq.a: Because the metal ring of a standard bonded seal is carbon steel, and in a stainless joint exposed to water or salt air it will rust and pit the faces it seals against. A stainless ring keeps the whole joint in one material. Replace bonded seals each time the joint is remade.

faq.q: What is a countersunk sealed plug?
faq.a: A plug whose head sits recessed, flush with the port face, sealed by a Viton seal rather than a taper thread. Use it where a projecting hex head would foul something; use a hex head plug where clearance allows easier removal. Match the plug to the port thread — BSPP or metric.

faq.q: Are these 316 stainless?
faq.a: Most families are 316L stainless steel, forged; each listing states the grade the manufacturer gives. Where a listing says stainless steel without a grade, ask and we will confirm before you order.

faq.q: Do the listings show dimensions and equivalents?
faq.a: Yes, where the manufacturer publishes them. Every size is listed with its end sizes; most also carry millimetre dimensions and the Parker part number the manufacturer cross-references.

faq.q: What is a street elbow?
faq.a: A pipe elbow with a male thread at one end and a female thread at the other, so it screws straight into a female port or fitting without a separate nipple. That saves one joint and some length in a tight run. Street tees work the same way, with one male end.

faq.q: Hex head, hex socket or hollow hex plug — which do I need?
faq.a: Choose by clearance and access. A hex head plug is turned with a spanner and stands proud of the port. A hex socket plug takes an Allen key and sits nearly flush, for tight spaces. A hollow hex head plug is lighter and takes either tool. All seal on the NPT taper and need thread sealant.

faq.q: What is the difference between NPT and NPTF?
faq.a: NPTF (dryseal) threads are made so the crests and roots meet as the joint tightens, designed to seal without sealant. Standard NPT leaves a spiral leak path at the crests and roots that sealant or tape must fill. The two screw together, but the joint then needs sealant like NPT. Stainless taper threads are prone to galling, so a sealant with anti-galling properties is commonly used.

faq.q: How tight should a stainless NPT fitting be?
faq.a: Typically hand tight plus two to three turns with a spanner, but follow the maker’s figure for the size. Over-tightening a taper thread can split a female port or gall the thread; under-tightening leaves a leak path. Each remake goes a little deeper, so a heavily reused taper end should be replaced.

categories.intro: Rigging hardware is the forged, cast and stainless fittings that join slings, chain and wire rope to a hook, a load or an anchor point: shackles, hooks, master links, rings, swivels, eye bolts, turnbuckles and lifting points. standards.heading: ASME B30.26 — rigging hardware
standards.body: ASME B30.26 covers detachable rigging hardware: shackles, links and rings, swivels, eye bolts, swivel hoist rings, turnbuckles, wire rope clips, wedge sockets and rigging blocks. It sets identification marking, training, pre-use and periodic inspection, and removal from service, and it requires replacement parts to meet the original manufacturer's specification. A shackle body, for example, must carry the maker's name or trademark, the rated load and the size, and the markings must stay legible for its service life. Hooks are covered separately by ASME B30.10.

faq.q: Which shackle do I need — anchor (bow) or chain (dee)?
faq.a: A chain (dee) shackle is for a straight, in-line pull. An anchor (bow) shackle has a rounder body that accepts more than one sling or a pull at an angle to the pin. For a permanent or long-term installation choose a bolt-type shackle, whose nut and cotter pin cannot unscrew in service; a screw-pin shackle suits rigging that is made and broken often.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Which rigging hardware is not meant for overhead lifting?
faq.a: Anything without a published working load limit for lifting. On this shelf that typically includes cold shut and repair links, S hooks, most snap hooks and quick links, lag screw and wire-turned eye bolts, DIN 444 swing bolts, strap staples and lashing D rings, and commercial-grade shackles. These are made for fencing, lashing, light connecting and general duty. If a product page gives no WLL, or gives a lashing capacity instead, treat the item as not rated for lifting and use a rated shackle, hook, master link or lifting point instead.

faq.q: Can I mix US-pattern and European-pattern fittings in one rig?
faq.a: Yes, provided every component is rated for the load it carries and the parts fit each other properly. Patterns differ in dimensions, so check the fit: a shackle pin must pass through a hook eye or lifting point without forcing, a master link must sit freely in the crane hook bowl, and no fitting should bear on another's tip or bind at an angle. The assembly is only as strong as its lowest-rated component, so rate the rig on that one, not on the heaviest part.

faq.q: Stainless, galvanised or alloy rigging hardware — which should I use?
faq.a: Choose on rating first, then on environment. Grade 8 alloy fittings carry the highest rating for their size and suit heavy lifting; galvanised carbon steel is the general choice outdoors; stainless suits splash zones, food plant and architectural rigging where rust staining is unacceptable. Do not assume a stainless or galvanised part has the same WLL as an alloy part of the same nominal size — ratings are set by each maker for each material, and the size table on the product page shows them as separate rows.

categories.intro: Shackles are U-shaped forged or cast connectors closed by a removable pin, used to join slings, chain and wire rope to a hook, lifting point or anchor. Indus supplies 46 shackle ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: screw-pin, round-pin and bolt-type anchor and chain shackles to the G-209, G-210, G-213, G-215, G-2130 and G-2150 patterns, Grade 8 alloy, AS 2741 Grade S, BS 3032, DIN 82101, European, Italian and JIS types, plus stainless shackles and snap shackles.

standards.heading: Patterns, RR-C-271 and ASME B30.26
standards.body: US pattern numbers such as G-209 trace to Federal Specification RR-C-271, which classes shackles by type, grade and class; makers state, for example, that G-209 screw-pin anchor shackles meet the performance requirements of RR-C-271 Type IVA, Grade A, Class 2. ASME B30.26 requires each new shackle body to be forged, cast or die-stamped with the maker's name or trademark, the rated load and the size, and the pin to be marked too. DIN 82101, BS 3032, AS 2741 and JIS shackles follow their own standards' dimensions and ratings.

faq.q: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
faq.a: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: When does a shackle have to be taken out of service?
faq.a: When ASME B30.26's removal criteria or the maker's instructions say so. The standard's list includes missing or illegible markings, heat damage, excessive pitting or corrosion, a bent, twisted, distorted or elongated body or pin, cracks, excessive nicks or gouges, damaged threads, incomplete pin engagement, unauthorised welding, and a reduction of 10% of the original or catalogue dimension at any point around the body or pin. A shackle removed for any of these returns to service only if a qualified person approves it.

faq.q: Can I replace a lost shackle pin with an ordinary bolt?
faq.a: No. Replace it only with the pin the shackle maker supplies for that size and grade. A shackle's rating depends on a pin of the right diameter, material and heat treatment, and a hardware bolt has none of these guaranteed; ASME B30.26 requires replacement parts to meet the original manufacturer's specification. Pins from another maker or pattern may look the same but differ in thread, length or grade, so they should not be swapped between shackles either.

faq.q: Carbon, Grade 8 alloy or stainless — which shackle should I order?
faq.a: Order the material your rigging plan rates for. A Grade 8 alloy shackle carries a higher WLL than a carbon-steel shackle of the same nominal size, so it is the usual choice where weight and size matter. Galvanised carbon-steel shackles are the general-purpose standard. Stainless shackles are chosen for corrosion, not strength, and their ratings vary by maker and casting. The size table on each product page lists the WLL for every size; compare those rows rather than the nominal size.

categories.intro: Lifting hooks are forged or cast hooks that carry a load, sling or chain leg on the bowl of the hook, and come as eye, clevis, shank and swivel types for hoisting, slip and grab duty. standards.heading: ASME B30.10 — hooks
standards.body: ASME B30.10 covers hooks on hoists, cranes and slings: marking, inspection and removal from service. Its removal criteria include distortion that increases the throat opening by more than 5%, not to exceed 1/4″, or as the manufacturer recommends; wear of more than 10% of the original section dimension of the hook or its load pin; any visible bend or twist from the plane of the unbent hook; cracks, nicks or gouges; and an inoperative or missing latch where one is required. AS/NZS 4344 is a load-restraint standard, not a lifting standard.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: What do the 319, 320, 322, 323, 324, 330 and 331 hook numbers mean?
faq.a: They are US pattern numbers that identify the hook's form. 319 is a shank hoist hook, 320 an eye hoist hook and 322 a swivel hoist hook; 323 is an eye grab hook, 324 an eye slip hook, 330 a clevis grab hook and 331 a clevis slip hook. An H or A prefix, and the -C or -A suffix in the Indus part number, separates the carbon and alloy versions of the same frame, which carry different ratings.

faq.q: Are the Grade 70 AS/NZS 4344 hooks rated for lifting?
faq.a: No. AS/NZS 4344 covers load restraint on vehicles, and hooks made to it are rated by lashing capacity for tie-down with Grade 70 transport chain. Use them on load binders and lashing chains, not in an overhead lift. For lifting, choose a hook with a published WLL for lifting, in the same grade as the chain it goes on, such as a Grade 80 or alloy-steel hook.

faq.q: Eye, clevis or shank hook — how do I choose the attachment?
faq.a: Choose by what the hook connects to. An eye hook hangs from a master link, shackle or sling eye through its forged eye. A clevis hook pins directly onto a chain link with its clevis pin, which keeps the assembly short, and must be the same grade and size as the chain. A shank hook is fitted into a hoist or block body and retained by a nut, and a swivel hook lets the load turn freely. Each type carries its own rating in the size table.

faq.q: Can I shorten a chain sling leg with a grab hook?
faq.a: Yes, with a grab hook made and rated for it, of the same grade as the chain. The grab hook holds a link edgeways in its narrow throat; a slip hook used this way lets the chain run and must not be used to shorten a leg. Some manufacturers apply a lower rating to a leg shortened with a grab hook that has no supporting cradle — check the maker's instructions for the hook you use.

categories.intro: Snap hooks and quick links are spring-gated or screw-closed connectors for clipping chain, rope, lanyards and light fittings together, used where a joint must be made and broken quickly. Indus supplies 44 ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: zinc-plated and stainless snap hooks, DIN 5299 carbine hooks with and without screw nut and eyelet, swivel eye bolt snaps, trigger and boat snaps, S hooks, and oval, pear, delta, long and wide-jaw quick links, galvanised and stainless.

guidance.heading: Duty first, then closure and material
guidance.body: Decide first whether the joint is part of a lift: if it is, use a rated shackle, hook or master link, not a snap hook. For light duty, choose the closure: a spring gate for fast, frequent connection; a screw nut or screw lock where the joint must not open by accident; a quick link where it stays closed for long periods. Then choose the shape for the connection, the eye type (fixed, swivel, round or square for webbing) and zinc-plated or stainless steel. To quote, send the form, material, size or WLL, and quantity.

faq.q: Are snap hooks and quick links for overhead lifting?
faq.a: Only within the WLL published for them, which is light — tens to hundreds of kilograms on most sizes. For lifting loads use rated shackles, hooks and master links.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Does a quick link carry its rated load with the sleeve open?
faq.a: No. A quick link is only rated with its threaded sleeve screwed fully closed, so the load passes through a closed ring. With the sleeve open it is a hook with no throat support and can open under very little load. Close the sleeve by hand until it seats and check it before each use, because vibration can back it off. A quick link is not a hinge or a substitute for a shackle in a lift.

faq.q: Can these snap hooks be used on a fall-arrest harness or lanyard?
faq.a: Not unless the product is certified as personal protective equipment. Connectors for fall protection must be tested and marked to a PPE standard such as EN 362 in Europe or ANSI Z359.12 in the US, with an auto-locking gate. The snap hooks and carbine hooks on this shelf are general-purpose hardware; if a product page does not state PPE certification, do not use it in a fall-arrest or work-positioning system.

faq.q: Oval, pear or delta quick link — what is the difference?
faq.a: Each shape suits a different connection. An oval quick link loads evenly along its long axis and suits a single in-line connection. A pear-shaped link has a wider end that gathers several ropes, straps or chain ends at one point. A delta (triangle) link has a flat base that lies a strap or webbing evenly and takes pulls from more than one direction. Wide-jaw links have a larger gate opening for thicker chain or fittings. Each carries the WLL its maker publishes for that shape and size.

faq.q: Which snap hook suits marine and boat use?
faq.a: Use stainless steel, and pick the gate for the job. A swivel eye bolt snap lets a line or lanyard turn without kinking; a trigger snap opens with one hand on a boat deck; a boat snap with a fixed eye suits a permanent rope end; a carbine hook with a screw nut closes a joint that must not open. Galvanised and zinc-plated hooks corrode quickly in salt spray. None of these is a lifting fitting unless the maker publishes a lifting WLL.

categories.intro: Eye bolts and eye nuts are threaded fittings with a forged or formed eye that screw into or onto a load to give a lifting or fixing point. Indus supplies 37 ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: DIN 580 eye bolts and DIN 582 eye nuts in metric and UNC threads, JIS B 1168 eye bolts and B 1169 eye nuts, BS 4278 collared, linked and dynamo eyebolts, US shoulder and regular nut eye bolts and G-275, G-279 and G-291 pattern eye bolts, in galvanised, zinc-plated and stainless steel.

standards.heading: DIN 580, DIN 582, JIS and BS 4278
standards.body: DIN 580 sets the dimensions and load table for metric lifting eye bolts with a collar, and DIN 582 the matching lifting eye nuts; JIS B 1168 and JIS B 1169 are the Japanese equivalents, and BS 4278 covers collared eyebolts (Table 1), collared eyebolts with link (Table 2) and dynamo eyebolts (Table 3). Each standard's table gives the WLL for a straight pull and reduced values for angled use. DIN 444 swing bolts and DIN 71752 clevis joints are fastening parts, not lifting fittings. ASME B30.26 covers eye bolts in US practice.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Are DIN 580, JIS B 1168, BS 4278 and US eye bolts interchangeable?
faq.a: Not reliably. Each standard has its own thread form, shank length, collar size and load table, so an eye bolt must match the tapped hole it goes into and carry its own published rating. A metric bolt will not seat properly in a UNC hole, and an eye bolt that does not seat fully on its collar or shoulder loses its angled rating. Order to the standard and thread of the hole — metric coarse, UNC or as marked on the equipment — and check the thread length against the hole depth.

faq.q: Which eye bolts on this shelf are not for lifting?
faq.a: Lag screw eyes, wood lag ring bolts, wire-turned welded and unwelded eye bolts, DIN 444 swing eye bolts and DIN 71752 clevis joints are made for fixing, fencing, guying and machine linkages, not for lifting. Use a forged eye bolt or eye nut with a published WLL, made to DIN 580, DIN 582, JIS B 1168, BS 4278 or a US forged pattern, and check its product page shows a lifting rating before rigging from it.

faq.q: How do I rig a two-leg lift from two eye bolts?
faq.a: Use shoulder or collared eye bolts, seated fully on their collars, with the plane of each eye lined up with its sling leg, and apply the reduced rating the maker's table gives for the angle. Never unscrew a bolt short of full seating to turn the eye into line; use the maker's permitted washers or shims, or change to a swivel lifting point. Plain-shank eye bolts are for vertical pulls only, and a spreader beam keeps the legs vertical where the angle would be too flat.

faq.q: When should I use an eye nut instead of an eye bolt?
faq.a: Use an eye nut where the load already has a protruding threaded stud or bolt, such as a machine or motor with a stud fitted for lifting, and an eye bolt where it has a tapped hole. An eye nut must be screwed fully home onto a stud long enough for full thread engagement and seated on a flat face. The same angle rules apply as for an eye bolt, so check the maker's table for anything other than a straight pull.

categories.intro: Master links, rings and swivels are the forged connecting pieces of a rigging assembly: a master link gathers sling legs onto the crane hook, rings and pear links join several pulls at one point, and swivels let the rigging untwist. Indus supplies 36 ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: weldless alloy master links, Grade 80 weldless forged rings, weldless pear links in carbon and alloy, G-401 and G-402 pattern swivels, Grade 80 regular and roller-bearing swivels, clevis links, and stainless rings, D rings and swivels.

guidance.heading: Size the link to the hook and to every leg
guidance.body: Start from the hook the link must hang on: the master link's inside length and width must let it seat freely in the hook bowl without binding. Then rate it for the total load of all legs, at the sling angle, in the same grade as the chain or fittings below it. For three- and four-leg slings use a master link assembly with intermediate links, not one large link. Cold shut and repair links are for chain repair and general duty, not overhead lifting. To quote, send the hook size, number of legs, WLL, grade and quantity.

standards.heading: EN 1677-4 and ASME B30.26
standards.body: EN 1677-4 covers Grade 8 links used as components of lifting slings — master links, master link sub-assemblies and intermediate links — and sits within the EN 1677 series of sling-component standards. ASME B30.26 covers links, rings and swivels as rigging hardware, with requirements for identification marking, inspection and removal from service. Galvanised chain swivels and malleable cleats are general marine and mooring fittings; rate them from the maker's data, not from these standards.

faq.q: Can a swivel rotate under load?
faq.a: A standard chain swivel lets the rigging untwist but is not designed to rotate while carrying its full load. Use it to prevent twisting, not as a rotating bearing.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: How big a master link do I need for my crane hook?
faq.a: One whose inside dimensions let it sit freely in the hook's bowl, and whose WLL covers the total load of every leg at the sling angle. A link that is rated high enough but too small will ride on the hook's tip or bind against its sides, and that loads both parts in a way neither is rated for. Check the hook's bowl dimensions against the link's inside length and width in the size table before ordering.

faq.q: Master link, ring or pear link — which should I use?
faq.a: Use a master link to hang a sling on a crane hook — its oblong shape seats in the hook bowl. Use a ring where pulls come from several directions at once, such as a rigging junction, since its round shape spreads the load. Use a pear link where several legs gather at the wide end and the narrow end goes on a hook. Each shape has its own rating for the same bar diameter, so compare WLLs, not sizes.

faq.q: What is a master link assembly for a three- or four-leg sling?
faq.a: It is a master link with two intermediate links fitted below it, so that three or four legs hang from two smaller links rather than crowding one. This keeps each leg's connecting link seated correctly and stops the legs bearing on each other. EN 1677-4 covers these sub-assemblies for Grade 8 slings. The assembly is rated as a unit; do not substitute a single oversized link.

faq.q: Are cold shut and repair links safe for lifting?
faq.a: No. Cold shut links and repair (lap) links are closed by hammering or bolting and are made for chain repair, fencing and general duty. They have no lifting rating unless the maker publishes one, and on this shelf they are zinc-plated general-duty parts. To join or repair lifting chain, use a grade-matched connecting link made for that chain.

categories.intro: Lifting points and pad eyes are anchorages fixed to a load or structure — bolted, threaded or welded — that give a sling a rated point to attach to. Indus supplies 32 ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: Grade 80 and Grade 100 swivel lifting points, swivel hoist rings and swivel eye nuts, Grade 80 DIN 580 eye bolts and DIN 582 eye nuts, bolt-on and weld-on points, weld-on D rings and pivoting D links, stainless pad eyes and eye plates, deck eye plates and lashing D rings.

standards.heading: ASME B30.26 and the DIN eye bolt standards
standards.body: ASME B30.26 covers swivel hoist rings and eye bolts as rigging hardware, including identification marking, inspection and removal from service. Grade 80 eye bolts and eye nuts on this shelf follow the DIN 580 and DIN 582 dimensions with the higher rating of their alloy grade, as published by the maker. Weld-on lifting points, pad eyes and deck plates have no single dimensional standard: their rating, weld size and base material come from the maker's instructions.

faq.q: Can I lift at an angle from an eye bolt?
faq.a: A plain eye bolt is rated for a straight pull along the thread axis; at an angle its capacity falls sharply. A shoulder eye bolt seated fully takes an angled pull at a reduced rating. Where the pull will be angled or will change direction, use a swivel lifting point, which turns to follow the sling.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: What thread engagement and torque does a bolt-on lifting point need?
faq.a: Exactly what its maker states for that size. A swivel hoist ring or bolt-on point is rated only when its bolt is tightened to the specified torque in a hole of sound thread and adequate depth, with the bushing or base seated flat on the load. The required engagement is longer in cast iron or aluminium than in steel, and the maker gives figures for each. Do not substitute a different bolt or omit the washer, and recheck torque if the point has been removed and refitted.

faq.q: How do I tell a lifting pad eye from a lashing pad eye?
faq.a: By its rating. A lifting point carries a WLL for lifting, stamped on it or stated by the maker, and comes with a certificate for that duty. Lashing D rings, deck eye plates and staples are rated for securing cargo — often as a lashing capacity in kN or daN, or not rated at all — and should not be lifted from. On this shelf, check the product page: if it gives no lifting WLL, the item is for lashing or fixing.

faq.q: What is a precast concrete lifting clutch used with?
faq.a: A lifting clutch hooks into a spread or lifting anchor cast into a precast concrete unit, and it works only with the anchor system it was designed for. Match the clutch to the anchor's head type and load class from the same system, and follow that system maker's rules for anchor embedment, edge distance and concrete strength at lift. Send the anchor make and load class when you request a quote.

categories.intro: Hoists, blocks and clamps are the below-the-crane and stand-alone devices that raise, move and grip a load: chain blocks, lever hoists and electric hoists lift it, trolleys carry a hoist along a beam, pulley and snatch blocks redirect rope, and plate and beam clamps grip steel. Indus supplies 147 items from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers, including VL, ORM and E type manual chain blocks, VA lever hoists, MD1 and 2/1-reeved electric wire rope hoists, push and geared trolleys, snatch and pulley blocks, and CDH, PDQ and TMS plate clamps.

standards.heading: Hoist and clamp standards
standards.body: In European practice, EN 13157 covers hand-powered lifting equipment such as chain blocks and lever hoists, EN 14492-2 power-driven hoists, and EN 13155 non-fixed load lifting attachments, which include plate clamps. In US practice, ASME B30.16 covers overhead hoists, B30.21 lever hoists and B30.20 below-the-hook lifting devices, including clamps. Each sets design, marking, inspection and operating requirements; the rated load and any test certificate for a given item come from its maker.

faq.q: What is the difference between a push trolley and a geared trolley?
faq.a: A push trolley is moved by pushing on the load; a geared trolley is driven by a hand chain, which gives finer positioning and is easier with heavier loads.

faq.q: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
faq.a: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Chain block or lever hoist — which do I need?
faq.a: Use a chain block for vertical lifting from an overhead anchor, where the operator can stand clear and pull the hand chain. Use a lever hoist for short lifts, pulling and tensioning, and for work in confined spaces or at angles, since it is operated by a ratchet lever and needs no hand-chain drop. Lever hoists can be used in orientations other than vertical where their maker permits it. Both are rated by capacity and lift; check the hook-to-hook headroom on the table.

faq.q: Vertical or horizontal plate clamp — which do I need?
faq.a: It depends on how the plate hangs during the lift. A vertical clamp grips one edge so a plate can hang vertically or be turned from flat to vertical, and is used singly or in pairs as its maker allows. Horizontal clamps grip the plate edge from below and are used in pairs or sets, on a spreader or multi-leg sling, to lift a plate held flat. Each clamp is rated for a plate thickness range as well as a maximum load, and some makers also set a minimum load, so check the clamp's table.

faq.q: What does 2/1 reeving mean on an electric wire rope hoist?
faq.a: It means the hook block hangs on two falls of rope rather than one. With 2/1 reeving each fall carries roughly half the load, so the hoist can lift more with the same rope and drum, but the hook moves at half the rope speed and the drum gives half the lift of a 1/1 arrangement. Rated capacity, speed and lift height for each reeving are on the product page.

categories.intro: Snatch blocks and pulley blocks are sheaved blocks that change the direction of a rope or multiply its pull; a snatch block has a side plate that opens so the rope can be laid in mid-length. Indus supplies 106 ranges from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers: light snatch blocks to the 404, 408, 409, 418 and 419 patterns, champion and super-champion blocks, metric snatch blocks with swivel hook from 0.5 to 5 t, steel, malleable-iron, wooden and stainless pulley blocks, gin blocks and die-cast pulleys.

guidance.heading: Rope, block load, then attachment
guidance.body: Start with the rope: its type and diameter decide the sheave — wire rope needs a steel sheave grooved for its diameter, fibre rope a block made for fibre. Next work out the block load, which is the line pull multiplied by a factor for the angle between the lead lines — up to twice the pull when the rope turns back on itself and the lead lines run parallel. Then choose the attachment — hook, shackle, eye or swivel — and the number of sheaves. Rate the anchor point for the block load too. To quote, send the rope type and diameter, the block load or line pull, the attachment and quantity.

standards.heading: ASME B30.26 — rigging blocks
standards.body: ASME B30.26 includes rigging blocks — snatch blocks and other sheaved blocks used with wire or fibre rope — within its scope, with requirements for identification marking, inspection and removal from service. The rated load of a block, and the rope size it accepts, are set by its maker. Pattern numbers such as 418, 419, 420, 421, 430 and 431 are maker series designations, not standards; blocks sold to a pattern share its dimensions and attachment type.

faq.q: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
faq.a: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: How do I work out the load on a snatch block when the rope turns less than 180°?
faq.a: Multiply the line pull by twice the cosine of half the angle between the two lead lines. With the lines parallel (a 180° turn) the factor is 2.0; with 60° between them it is about 1.73, at 90° about 1.41, at 120° 1.0 and at 150° about 0.52. The block, its hook or shackle and the anchor point must each be rated for that resultant load, not for the line pull.

faq.q: What is the difference between a snatch block and a pulley block?
faq.a: A snatch block has a side plate that swings or slides open, so the rope can be laid into the sheave at any point along its length without threading the end through. A pulley block is closed, and the rope end has to be reeved through it. Snatch blocks are used to redirect a winch or hoist line; closed blocks are used in fixed tackles and reeved purchases.

faq.q: Can I run wire rope through a pulley made for fibre rope?
faq.a: No. Blocks are made for one kind and size of rope. Wire rope needs a steel sheave with a groove that matches its diameter and a sheave large enough for that rope; a wooden-shell, nylon or fibre-rope block has a groove and sheave diameter suited to fibre rope, and wire rope will damage the sheave and itself. Check the rope type and diameter marked on the block or in the size table before reeving.

faq.q: Hook, shackle or swivel eye — which snatch block attachment should I choose?
faq.a: Choose on how the block is anchored and how often it is moved. A hook with a latch is quickest to rig and re-rig; a shackle stays captive on its anchor and suits a block that will stay in place or might otherwise jump off; a swivel eye or swivel hook lets the block turn to line up with the rope, and a fixed eye holds it in one plane. Whichever you choose, it must be rated for the full block load, not the line pull.

categories.intro: Lifting and general-purpose chain is welded round-link steel chain, graded by strength and tolerance, used with matching hooks and links to lift, hoist, lash or convey. Indus supplies Grade 80 and Grade 100 alloy lifting chain and fittings, EN 818-7 hoist chain, stainless chain, Grade 30, 43 and 70 chain in inch and AS/NZS 4344 sizes, DIN 763, 764 and 766 link chain and DIN 22252 mining chain, from Dubai under IH-LR part numbers.

standards.heading: Which standard covers which chain
standards.body: In Europe, Grade 8 medium-tolerance chain for slings is made to EN 818-2 and the finished sling to EN 818-4; fine-tolerance hoist chain is EN 818-7, and Grade 8 forged hooks and links fall under EN 1677. In the US, ASTM A391 covers Grade 80 alloy chain, ASTM A973 Grade 100, and ASTM A952 the forged Grade 80 and 100 fittings. Grade 70 chain on this shelf is also offered to AS/NZS 4344, the Australian load-restraint standard. DIN 763, 764 and 766 set the dimensions of general-purpose link chain and are not alloy lifting-chain standards.

faq.q: Can Grade 30, 43 or 70 chain be used for lifting?
faq.a: No. Proof coil (Grade 30), high test (Grade 43) and transport (Grade 70) chain are made for tie-down, towing and general duty. Overhead lifting with chain calls for alloy chain — Grade 80 or Grade 100 — with fittings of the same grade.

faq.q: Can I mix Grade 80 chain with Grade 100 fittings?
faq.a: A chain sling is rated by its weakest component, so a mixed assembly takes the lower grade's rating. Match the fittings to the chain grade and size.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: What is the difference between EN 818-2 and EN 818-7 chain?
faq.a: EN 818-2 is medium-tolerance Grade 8 chain for chain slings, and EN 818-7 is fine-tolerance chain made to run over the pocketed load sheave of a hoist. Hoist chain is calibrated so each link seats in the pocket, and it is specified by the hoist maker for that block. Sling chain does not have that pitch accuracy and must never be fitted to a hoist; hoist chain is not normally used to make up slings either. Order hoist chain by the hoist make and model as well as size.

faq.q: How can I tell what grade a lifting chain is?
faq.a: Alloy lifting chain is embossed at intervals along its length with a grade mark and the manufacturer's identification, and the fittings carry their own grade and size marks. Grade 80 chain is typically marked 8 or 80 and Grade 100 chain 10 or 100. If a chain carries no legible grade mark and no certificate traces it, treat it as unrated and keep it out of lifting service. Plain or galvanized chain with no mark is usually general-purpose chain.

faq.q: When should alloy lifting chain be taken out of service?
faq.a: Take it out of service when any link is worn, stretched, bent, nicked, cracked or heat-damaged beyond the manufacturer's limits, or when its grade and size marks can no longer be read. Manufacturers commonly set the wear limit at 10% loss of the link's nominal diameter, measured as the mean of two diameters at right angles. Any visible stretch, a link that no longer hinges freely, or weld spatter and heat discolouration are also reasons to remove it. The competent person's thorough examination is the deciding check.

categories.intro: Grade 80 chain fittings are forged alloy-steel hooks, master links and connectors rated to match Grade 80 chain of the same size, used to build chain slings and other lifting assemblies. Indus supplies eye, clevis and swivel sling hooks with latch or positive locking latch, grab, shortening, foundry, C and barrel hooks, master links and assemblies to EN 1677-4, welded master links, and Italian, European, US and metric connecting links, from Dubai.

guidance.heading: Choosing a Grade 80 fitting
guidance.body: Start with the job the fitting does: a sling hook with latch for general lifting, a positive or self-locking hook where the load must not come off, a grab or shortening hook to adjust leg length, a foundry hook where a latch would get in the way. Then the attachment: a clevis fitting pins straight onto the chain; an eye fitting needs a connecting link. Size every fitting to the chain size, not to the load, and for multi-leg slings pick the master link or assembly rated for the number of legs. To quote, send the chain size, grade, fitting type, attachment, quantity and any certification needed.

standards.heading: EN 1677 and ASTM A952
standards.body: EN 1677 covers Grade 8 forged components for slings: Part 1 general requirements, Part 2 hooks with latch, Part 3 self-locking hooks and Part 4 links. Grade 8 components are rated at a 4:1 design factor, with a manufacturing proof force of 2.5 times the working load limit and a minimum breaking force of 4 times it. In the US, ASTM A952 covers forged Grade 80 and Grade 100 lifting components. Each size table gives the WLL the manufacturer publishes for that fitting.

faq.q: Can I mix Grade 80 chain with Grade 100 fittings?
faq.a: A chain sling is rated by its weakest component, so a mixed assembly takes the lower grade's rating. Match the fittings to the chain grade and size.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Should I choose a clevis or an eye fitting?
faq.a: Choose a clevis fitting to pin directly onto the chain, or an eye fitting where you want to join it to the chain or a master link with a connecting link. A clevis fitting has no extra component in the load path and gives a shorter, neater sling. An eye fitting is useful for swapping hooks or joining to something a clevis pin cannot reach, such as a wire rope sling eye. Both must be the same grade and sized for the chain.

faq.q: What is the difference between a sling hook, a grab hook and a foundry hook?
faq.a: A sling hook has a wide throat to take a lifting point or a sling eye, a grab hook has a narrow slot that grips a chain link to shorten or choke a leg, and a foundry hook has a wide, open throat with no latch. Foundry hooks are for handling moulds and ladles where a latch would foul. Some manufacturers derate a leg shortened on a grab hook without a cradle or support, so check the size table before relying on full WLL.

faq.q: When do I need a self-locking or positive locking hook rather than a latch hook?
faq.a: Use a self-locking or positive locking hook where the sling could go slack or the load could shift and lift the eye out of the hook. On a standard sling hook the spring latch only keeps a slack sling in place; it is not a load-bearing part. A self-locking hook closes and locks under load and opens only when the operator releases it, which suits lifts where the rigger cannot see the hook or the load may snag.

faq.q: Can Grade 80 fittings be welded, heated or ground?
faq.a: No. Grade 80 fittings get their strength from quenching and tempering, and welding, heating or grinding can destroy it without any visible sign. Do not weld lugs to a hook, straighten a bent fitting with heat or grind out a nick unless the manufacturer's instructions allow it. A fitting that has been exposed to welding arcs, heat or chemical attack should be removed from service and examined.

categories.intro: Grade 100 chain fittings are forged alloy-steel hooks, links and connectors rated to match Grade 100 chain, which carries about 25% more than Grade 80 chain of the same size. Indus supplies Grade 100 clevis, eye and swivel sling hooks, OBK, LBK and GBK self-locking hooks, grab, cradle, plate, foundry and forest hooks, shortening clutches, master links and assemblies, oversized master links and chain connectors, from Dubai.

faq.q: Can I mix Grade 80 and Grade 100 components?
faq.a: You can, but the sling is then rated as Grade 80: the weakest component sets the working load limit of the whole assembly. To use the Grade 100 rating, every component in the load path must be Grade 100.

faq.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faq.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faq.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
faq.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

faq.q: Is there a European standard for Grade 100 fittings?
faq.a: Not as such: EN 1677 covers Grade 8 forged components, and Grade 100 fittings are generally rated by the manufacturer on the same 4:1 method. In the US, ASTM A952 covers forged Grade 80 and Grade 100 lifting components. Because the rating comes from the maker rather than a European dimension standard, Grade 100 fittings from different makers are not guaranteed to fit each other's chain pins and links. Keep to one maker's system within a sling and work to the WLL in the size table.

faq.q: What do OBK, LBK, GBK and EGKN mean on Grade 100 hooks?
faq.a: They are pattern names used in European hook ranges, and on this shelf the main difference is how the hook attaches. OBK is the eye-type self-locking hook with grip latch, LBK the swivel type and GBK the clevis type; EGKN is a clevis sling hook with a forged latch. Quote the pattern name together with the chain size when ordering a replacement, since dimensions and latch design differ between patterns.

faq.q: When do I need an oversized master link?
faq.a: Use an oversized or large-inside-length master link when the standard master link for your chain size will not sit freely in the crane hook. A master link must seat in the bowl of the hook without being forced or bearing on the hook tip.
